scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Independent ten-item B2 assessment draft for The Last Cup: A Film That Does Not Let Us Look Away; human pedagogy approval required.

tabs.title: Applying the Argument
tabs.description: Use the text in new situations.

questions.q: What makes the red cup an effective opening image for the reviewer?
choices: It proves that every concert hall has a serious waste problem.
It identifies the person who is responsible for recycling.
It represents rubbish that remains when the celebration is over.
It shows that the documentary uses only invented scenes.
questions.explanation: The discarded cup stands for waste normally ignored after an event, although the reviewer questions the reliance on images.

questions.q: Why does the reviewer favour the street cleaner's conversation over dramatic wildlife imagery?
choices: It makes waste management a practical question of time, resources and people.
It offers a more emotional appeal without giving any numbers.
It proves that animal pollution is less important than city cleaning.
It shows the film is mainly about the career of a cleaner.
questions.explanation: The conversation reveals a real timetable, budget and people working on solutions.

questions.q: What is implied by the director's refusal to mock the teenagers' first chaotic evening?
choices: The director thinks their plan was perfectly organised.
The director believes mistakes should be hidden from viewers.
The concert should have been cancelled until everything worked.
The director allows imperfect experiments to be part of meaningful action.
questions.explanation: Paragraph three values filming practical mistakes sympathetically rather than presenting flawless action.

questions.q: Why does the reviewer criticise the film's advice about reusable cups?
choices: It overlooks that reusable cups can never be cleaned safely.
It treats a choice as simple even where rules or facilities make it difficult.
It assumes teenagers are uninterested in environmental issues.
It suggests that single-use bottles cost more in every case.
questions.explanation: The reviewer cites security restrictions and limited washing facilities as overlooked barriers.

questions.q: Why is the deposit scheme described as the documentary 'at its best'?
choices: Its success is guaranteed after the first summer.
The documentary avoids showing how much it costs.
It presents an option alongside costs, uncertainties and further measurements.
It proves that every guest is willing to return a borrowed cup.
questions.explanation: The scheme includes transparent cost data and important limitations rather than a simple promise.

questions.q: What is the point of the imagined question about who will empty the bins next Friday?
choices: It highlights the need for sustained practical organisation beyond a hopeful ending.
It suggests the final beach concert should move to another venue.
It criticises the teenagers for not making an exciting film.
It shows that rubbish removal is only a problem on Fridays.
questions.explanation: The review wants operational follow-through rather than relying on a beautiful final image.

questions.q: How does the review distinguish a social barrier from an 'excuse'?
choices: It says personal responsibility has no role in waste reduction.
It argues that viewers should always choose the cheapest product.
It claims that only organisers are responsible for the cups.
It asks the film to investigate real constraints before judging individuals.
questions.explanation: The reviewer wishes the director had explored security and washing problems rather than dismissing them.

questions.q: A school wants to introduce reusable cups. Which plan best matches the reviewer's preferred approach?
choices: Announce that everyone must bring a cup and consider no exceptions.
Test a deposit system and publish its costs, returns and washing needs.
Show pictures of clean beaches without changing the event plan.
Purchase the most expensive reusable cups immediately.
questions.explanation: The strongest example is a tested scheme with transparent measurements and costs.

questions.q: Students discover that the cheapest supplier uses disposable bottles. What response follows the film's useful example?
choices: Choose the supplier and keep the packaging problem private.
Cancel the event rather than test an alternative.
Try accessible shared containers and learn from early difficulties.
Ask the guests not to drink anything during the event.
questions.explanation: The teenagers borrow jugs and ask guests to bring cups, experimenting despite an imperfect first evening.

questions.q: What would make a class discussion of the film most valuable?
choices: Question both its practical solutions and the obstacles it underplays.
Decide whether the final shoreline image is attractive enough.
List the interviewees' names without considering their points.
Agree that every environmental problem is an individual failure.
questions.explanation: The conclusion recommends viewing critically and continuing the practical discussion.
